summary:
KrishiMitra helps farmers in Madhya Pradesh, India, compare crop rotations for the next season. Farmers select their field, enter what they know about their soil and water supply, and set priorities such as conserving water or improving soil health. The app compares rotations side by side and explains the trade-offs so farmers can discuss their options with a local agricultural adviser.

KrishiMitra uses NASA MODIS observations to show historical vegetation greenness, NASA POWER weather data to support historical water planning, and ESA WorldCover to display mapped cropland. It combines this context with farmer inputs and agronomic rules to explain how different rotations fit a farm’s priorities.

The app supports English and Hindi, lets farmers save plans and seasonal records, and includes Sumiti, a voice-enabled assistant. Water figures are planning estimates, and the experimental yield model needs validation with local field records before it can guide decisions for individual farms.
details:
KrishiMitra is a crop rotation planning tool built by Team NavicNodes for farmers in Madhya Pradesh, India. It addresses the Field Shift — Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge by helping farmers compare what to grow next based on their field conditions, available water, and priorities.

A farmer searches for their town, selects a field on the map, and enters what they know about their soil, water supply, and past crops. They can then set priorities such as conserving water or improving soil health. KrishiMitra compares crop sequences side by side and explains the factors behind each option. Farmers can save plans and seasonal records, use the app in English or Hindi, and ask Sumiti, the voice-enabled assistant, for help navigating the tool.

The project’s creative contribution is bringing Earth observations and farmers’ own knowledge into the same decision. NASA MODIS shows historical vegetation greenness, NASA POWER provides weather data for historical water planning, and ESA WorldCover 2021 shows areas classified as cropland. Agronomic rules use farmer inputs and crop characteristics to explain why a rotation may suit a farm and where it involves a trade-off. This gives farmers concrete options to discuss with a local agricultural adviser.

We built the web app with React and Vite, an Express API on Node.js, and a Python service that retrieves geospatial data through Google Earth Engine. Users can access it through a web browser with no dedicated hardware.

We considered seasonal crop timing, soil conditions, water availability, and the farmer’s goals. We also considered how much the data can tell us about an individual field. Satellite observations can cover an area larger than the farm, so local measurements remain valuable. Water figures are historical planning estimates, and the experimental yield model needs validation with local field records before it can guide decisions for individual farms. The intended impact is to help farmers make better-informed rotation choices that support soil health and use available water more carefully.
